entities.name: Chapter 1
entities.description: Chapter 1 introduces high-temperature materials and superalloys, covering their background, characteristics, applications in gas turbine engines, material selection methods including the Larson-Miller approach, historical development, and justification for using nickel as a high-temperature material. entities.description: In 1967, large land-based industrial gas turbines featured a turbine inlet temperature of 900°C, a pressure ratio of 10.5, an exhaust temperature of 427°C, cooling applied only to the R1 vane, a power rating of 50–60 MW, a simple cycle efficiency of 29%, and a combined cycle efficiency of 43%.

In 1972, large land-based industrial gas turbines operated with a turbine inlet temperature of 1010°C, a pressure ratio of 11, an exhaust temperature of 482°C, cooling on R1 and R2 vanes and R1 blade, a power rating of 60–80 MW, a simple cycle efficiency of 31%, and a combined cycle efficiency of 46%.

By 1979, large land-based industrial gas turbines achieved a turbine inlet temperature of 1120°C, a pressure ratio of 14, an exhaust temperature of 530°C, cooling extended to R1 and R2 vanes and blades, a power rating of 70–105 MW, a simple cycle efficiency of 34%, and a combined cycle efficiency of 49%.
